title: Drug-Resistant Superbug Candida Auris Tops 3,000 Cases Across 23 U.S. States
excerpt: The deadly fungus, which can resist last-resort antifungal medications, is spreading through hospitals and nursing homes at an accelerating pace, with Texas, Michigan, and Illinois reporting the highest caseloads.
body:
• The CDC has recorded 3,130 confirmed cases of the drug-resistant fungus Candida auris across 23 U.S. states through July 18, 2026, putting the country on pace to exceed last year's total of 3,348 cases.
  • Texas leads with 706 cases — already surpassing its entire 2025 total — followed by Michigan with 503 and Illinois with 366.
  • The fungus is multidrug-resistant, with some strains resisting even amphotericin B, a last-resort antifungal, and it spreads primarily in hospitals and nursing homes among severely ill patients.
  • The CDC classifies C. auris as an "urgent antimicrobial resistance threat," though the risk to the general public remains low.

A drug-resistant fungus classified as an "urgent threat" by federal health authorities is spreading through U.S. healthcare facilities at an accelerating pace, with more than 3,000 confirmed cases already recorded this year across 23 states.

The Numbers

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reported 3,130 screening cases of Candida auris through July 18, according to the agency's National Notifiable Diseases Surveillance System. That figure puts 2026 on track to surpass the 3,348 total cases recorded during the same period last year.

Texas has emerged as the epicenter, reporting 706 cases so far — more than it logged in all of 2025, when the state recorded 660. Michigan follows with 503 cases, then Illinois at 366 and Ohio at 271, per state and CDC data compiled by People and the Cincinnati Enquirer.

New York State, once the nation's hotspot for the fungus, has reported zero cases in 2026, though neighboring New Jersey has tallied 166.

Why C. Auris Is Different

First identified in a Japanese patient in 2009, C. auris has become one of the most alarming pathogens in modern infectious disease. Unlike common Candida yeast infections, this species is frequently multidrug-resistant, spreading easily in healthcare settings and surviving on surfaces for weeks.

"What makes Candida auris especially concerning is its resistance profile," said Nathan Wiederhold, director of the Fungus Testing Laboratory at the University of Texas at San Antonio. "Many strains are resistant to azoles, one of our major antifungal drug classes, and some are also resistant to amphotericin B, which is often considered a drug of last resort."

"The rapid emergence around the world and the speed of spread in the U.S. is alarming."

— Susan Huang, Professor of Infectious Diseases, UC Irvine School of Medicine

The estimated mortality rate among those infected is up to 60%, though many patients are already critically ill from other conditions when they contract the fungus.

How It Spreads

C. auris transmits through direct contact with infected individuals or contaminated surfaces in healthcare facilities. Patients most at risk are those reliant on invasive medical equipment — breathing tubes, feeding tubes, or catheters — or those with a history of heavy antibiotic or antifungal use, according to the Cleveland Clinic.

The fungus is often transmitted by asymptomatic carriers, making containment particularly difficult. Symptoms, when they appear, are generic — fever, chills, fatigue, low blood pressure, and elevated heart rate — and can be easily confused with other conditions, delaying diagnosis.

"Fungal infections are often overlooked because they are not as common as bacterial infections," Wiederhold said. "But they can be much more difficult to diagnose and treat, and we're seeing increasing spread and resistance."

Healthcare Response

The New York State Department of Health, working with the CDC, has been at the forefront of surveillance and containment efforts. The department recommends that healthcare facilities contact regional epidemiologists when C. auris is confirmed or suspected and follow CDC infection prevention protocols.

Interfacility communication about a patient's C. auris status is considered critical to preventing spread during patient transfers between hospitals and nursing homes. The CDC added C. auris to its notifiable diseases system to improve tracking across state lines.

What the Public Should Know

The CDC emphasizes that the risk to healthy individuals outside healthcare settings remains low. C. auris primarily threatens people who are already hospitalized or in long-term care facilities with serious underlying conditions.

For the Indian American community, the concern is practical rather than alarmist: families with elderly relatives in nursing homes or family members undergoing extended hospital stays should be aware of the fungus and can ask healthcare providers about facility-level C. auris protocols. Awareness is the first line of defense in a pathogen that thrives on institutional blind spots.

What's Next

With cases accumulating faster than containment measures can spread, public health officials are watching whether the fall and winter season — when hospital occupancy typically rises — will accelerate transmission. The development of new antifungal drugs, including the recently approved rezafungin, offers some hope, but the pipeline remains thin against a pathogen that evolves resistance faster than most fungi.
